abstract: A Revelio Labs research note by Loujaina Abdelwahed asking whether AI certifications pay off, built from a two-level taxonomy of over 500,000 unique AI-related certification names appearing on workers' public professional profiles. The piece documents an explosive rise in AI credentialing since ChatGPT and then tests whether certification holders actually do better. Its central and easily misread finding is that the raw salary advantage of certification holders is largely positive selection: the workers who choose to certify were already out-earning their peers in the same occupation and seniority level. Revelio is explicit that its results are correlational.
keyFindings: "After controlling for occupation and seniority level, AI certification holders earn, on average, an $8,000 salary premium compared to non-certification holders."
Revelio reads that gap as selection, not return: "within any given occupation and seniority level, the workers choosing to get certifications are those who are already earning more than their peers."

"The share of AI certifications among all professional credentials has increased over 20x since ChatGPT launched" — from roughly 1-2% of all professional certifications in 2018-2023 to nearly 30% by 2026.
"In order to understand the surge in AI certifications, we build a two-level taxonomy for over 500,000 unique AI-related certification names from workers' profiles."

On a propensity-score-matched comparison, "certification takers see their salary grow by 18.1% on average in their next position, compared to 15.3% for non-certification takers—a 2.8-percentage-point advantage."
Certification takers are modestly more mobile: 78.5% versus 76.1% change roles in their next transition, and 38.9% versus 32.5% move into a higher-seniority role.
methodology: AI certifications are identified by keyword search of certification titles on workers' public professional profiles, excluding academic degrees and focusing on non-degree certifications and courses. Over 500,000 unique certification names are organised into a two-level taxonomy. Salary comparisons control for occupation and seniority level. Outcome comparisons use a control group of non-certification takers constructed by propensity score matching on role, seniority, tenure, salary, AI exposure, and state.
qualifiers: The $8,000 figure is a within-occupation, within-seniority adjusted difference, not a raw gap and not a causal return to certification. Revelio publishes no base salary level, no sample size, no standard error and no currency year alongside it, so it cannot be converted into a percentage premium and therefore cannot be plotted on the high-skill wage premium graph, whose unit is percent premium over median. It is carried as an overlay for that reason and for a second, more important one: Revelio presents the number as evidence of positive selection into certifying, so plotting it as the value of a certification would invert the author's own meaning. Their closing caveat is explicit: "Propensity score matching does not fully eliminate this gap. Some of the mobility advantages we observe may reflect the underlying ambition and capability of those who choose to certify, rather than the effect of certification itself... results should be interpreted as correlations rather than causal." The 20x figure is a rise in certification share, not in certification count. The underlying population is workers with public professional profiles, which carries the profile-mutability caveat documented by Bloom et al. (NBER, 2026).
